narrative:
Your situation is genuinely interesting because the three strongest factors in your assessment actually worked in your favor, and understanding this can help you see why you still ended up in the remedial group. The model placed your chance of failing at 31 percent, which means you carry meaningful risk even though most signals seem positive. That is why the school has required these extra courses: they are meant to reduce that risk before it becomes real.

The most influential factor in the model was your record of past course failures. Since you have never failed a class, this strongly pushed the prediction toward passing, and it is a real strength you should be proud of. The second most important factor was your wish to pursue higher education. This too pulled toward a passing outcome, because students with that goal tend to stay motivated and engaged, even when work gets hard. The third factor was your mother’s work in services. Compared with other family backgrounds in the data, this was also linked to better chances, and it again moved the prediction in your favor.

So why the fail warning? Because other patterns outweighed these strengths. You study fewer than two hours each week, while most students who passed spent two hours or more. Your commute stretches beyond sixty minutes, which is very rare among successful students. You also reported very high free time, very frequent outings with friends, and especially high weekend alcohol consumption, far above what is typical for those who passed. These habits shifted the balance against you.

Consider building a steady study routine, using your long commute for review, and trimming weekend drinking and social outings. With your clean record and clear ambitions, small changes could make your outcome very different.
